$comment: What the Agenda (catalogue/agenda.html) reads on its first view, in one file: per demo its facts, fingerprint and update, per archived demo its decision, the pixel checks that reopen, and every catalogue block with its hash. Written by node gates/generate-agenda-index.mjs; the gate refuses a commit that leaves it stale. Anything missing here is read live.

facts.askText: You rejected seven settings sections for misalignment: a second column that was not uniform, rows off their labels, and “Send test” off the line of “Format” and “Minify”. The package now has one layout for all of these, .kp-formgrid: four columns, label, control, value and actions, that every row shares, so things line up by construction rather than by care. 6 sections, formal only; the content is made up. Every section names its grid under The grid. The project threads move their own pages onto it once you approve it, and a new measurement holds every demo to it.

Your rule is that a failed, empty or loading component fills the whole size it has with its data, centred, with a normal-size Retry, and the loading card sits over the whole component. The gaps the projects found were components that did not follow it: the network graph, the data table, the heat grid and matrix, the run timeline, the week agenda, a group of uptime strips and the card’s notes. They all use the package’s one state plate and loading card now. 8 sections, formal only (every fix is the theme’s own plate and loading card, so the other themes follow). Each section says under What changed since you approved it what was wrong and what is different now. Press a state under the section’s title to see it.

A choice a page could make with an attribute (segments or a menu, where a pill stands, how a table sorts, how a palette matches) was read once, when the component appeared, so changing the attribute later did nothing. Your rule (17/10) is that such a variant is an option with a default that switches at runtime. These ten components now do, and the refresh control also stops ignoring Refresh now, the R key and Retry now while it is paused. 10 pairs in all, formal only. In each section the buttons above the component set the very attribute a page would set; the component follows at once, and the line under it shows the effect. Each section says under What changed since you approved it what was wrong and what is different now.

Three parts of the homelab admin dashboard rebuilt on kp-themes 11.0.0, 24 sections in formal: the Settings page (staged changes with a Save bar, editors that fit each kind of key, links to one setting, a "This browser" card), the sign-in and secrets pages (passkeys, machine tokens, a QR to register a phone, reveal with an audit line, the secrets list and its change drawer, restart order, which file feeds which app) and the frame around every page (the connection banner, the folding bar, the slim rail, keys that work on a Belgian keyboard, problems, page states, effects).

The Activity page answers "what happened to my stacks, and what keeps failing". The Jobs page answers "what is running or waiting right now". Today both draw their own timeline, their own failure list and a "Show N more" feed. This page shows them on kp-themes 11.0.0: a run timeline you drag across, a grid of stack by day that shows which stack is flaky, a History table with day groups and openable rows, a Jobs timeline whose waiting time is visible, and the detail of one job.

The part of the recipe app that carries someone through a dish without asking them to hold the sequence in their head. It starts with one small step (gather the things), shows one cooking step at a time, keeps every timer running where it can be seen, and asks for attention only when something is done. The sample dish is Spaghetti with tomato sauce and meatballs, where the pasta and the sauce run at the same time. The timers here run fast (1 minute lasts 3 seconds) so you can watch them end; Real time is one button away. All data is mock.

You decided a loading picture for the network graph in every theme (character-graph, 2026-10-06), but the package only had one generic pulse for all of them, and kyu’s overview showed it. Now each theme draws its own: 12 pairs, one section per theme. Each section says under What changed since you approved it which picture you chose and how the graph looked before.

The Metrics page shows how hard the host pve and each stack are working, with what the host did marked on every chart. This page rebuilds its charts, its time window, its key figures, its drives and its traffic from the package's own parts, in formal. Each section asks one thing to look at and carries its options as defaults you can flip; nothing is required.

The Schedules page of the homelab admin dashboard decides what runs by itself: backups, updates, a weekly patch round, a restore test. This page shows how it would look with kp-themes 11.0.0, one part per section: the week, the next run with its countdown, the form that makes a schedule, the table, pausing, the busy minutes, the coverage and the history.

The screen for the moment you freeze on “what do we eat tonight”. The wheel chooses and you only say yes or spin again; filters keep the wheel to what fits; a No energy today switch cuts it down to dishes that ask almost nothing of you. The dishes are sample data (Belgian home cooking), the clock stands at Sunday 18/10/2026 17:10 and dinner is at 18:30. Judge it in the review dialog, in formal.

Time blindness means “I have plenty of time” is true until it suddenly is not. The app answers it backwards: you say when you eat, it works out when each part of the meal has to start, shows it as lanes you can see at a glance, shrinks the wait to the start as a disc instead of ticking numbers, and nudges you once, kindly. The sample dish is spaghetti with meatballs; the step times are mock data and nothing is saved. The page runs on a demo clock that starts at 17:22 on 18/10/2026.

The Inbox is where the homelab tells you what needs you: a question from the host, something that failed, an app with a newer version, a stack that needs setting up, a check only a person can answer. Notification rules decide what reaches your phone and when. This page shows both pages rebuilt on kp-themes 11.0.0, in seven sections: the list and its triage keys, ticking many rows at once, a question from the host with its clock, the manual checks one by one, the delivery rules, the routing per kind and per stack, and quiet hours.

The screen of a recipe app for someone with AuDHD: the recipe with its amounts that follow the number of portions, a big Begin cooking button, a code that opens cook mode on the phone, a printable sheet, the calm switch with theme and language, a cooking log in which an empty week is quiet, and the states of the page. Nothing here counts, scores or judges: no streaks, no red for a day without cooking. The recipe is a Belgian one (witloof in the oven); the dates are sample dates, today is Friday 16/10/2026 in this demo.

The screen for a day with no energy. Five parts, each answering one question without asking for effort: which dishes always work, what is in the freezer, what can be eaten without cooking, how a recipe shrinks to its smallest version, and when things went in. Nothing here counts calories or weight, nothing turns red, and every action can be taken back. This page asks formal only. The dish names and dates are sample content; the portions, the clock and the server are pretend.

Almanac turns events from Home Assistant, the homelab, kyu and AI sessions into Google Calendar entries. This is its Calendars page rebuilt on kp-themes 11.0.0 in formal: the header and counts, the attention band, the calendars table with its typed delete, the new-calendar dialog, the profile files and the uses map (feat-ui-1). 7 sections, 7 pairs. The data is sample data apart from the version and the totals; each section says which parts are made up.

The two sections Almanac builds itself on the status page, drawn with kp-themes 11.0.0 parts. Four sections, formal only. The numbers on the first card start from the live service on 19/10/2026 (version 4.1.7, up 10 days 3 h, 3 events accepted, 3 delivered, 0 failed, nothing pending). Anything beyond that is sample data and says so on the page.

Three new pages for Almanac's Status area, built from kp-themes 11.0.0 parts and shown in formal only. The numbers of the healthy chain are the live service's on 19/10/2026 (version 4.1.7: 3 events accepted, 3 delivered, 0 failed, 0 dead). Every outage, every waiting entry and every time on the schedule is sample data, labelled as such under each part; the timing rules (15 s, 1 min, 5 min, 15 min, then every 30 min; set aside after the third permanent refusal) are Almanac's real ones from src/core/pacing.rs and src/shell/worker.rs.

Two new Almanac pages in one demo: Try a source (paste an event call, see exactly what Almanac would put in the calendar, nothing is written) and the source profile view. The page is built from kp-themes 11.0.0 parts only, in formal. It never calls a server: the answers come from a small port of Almanac’s own dry-run rules (engine.js), checked against the two pinned fixtures byte for byte. Sample data: only home-assistant is a real profile name; the other three sources, every calendar id and the event already in the calendar are made up. Today is 19/10/2026.

HTTPSwitchboard accepts a message in one shape and delivers it in another; here the messages are Alertmanager alerts and the destination is Home Assistant. Two pages the service does not have yet, both new use cases found while planning its move to kp-themes 11.0.0: Try a translation (see what a profile makes of a message without sending anything to Home Assistant) and the history of reloads of the profile file (today a refused reload is only in the log and in a metric).

Two calendar views of what Almanac wrote into Google Calendar, built from the package’s month heatmap and week agenda. Sample data: the live service (4.1.7, up 10 days 3 h on 19/10/2026) has accepted and delivered 3 events and failed none; every event row on this page is mock so the views have something to show. The calendars (Almanac · Huishouden, Almanac · Infra, almanac-test) are the real names; the source named home-assistant is real, the others (homelab, kyu, claude-sessions) are mock names.

Round 2 of the kit pages: only what is still open. The issue and the manage dialog of the clients page are redrawn as grid compositions (round 1 was rejected for plain left/right alignment); the login page and the two passkeys pages were not judged in round 1 and come back unchanged. Everything else was approved and has left the page. In formal. 5 sections, 5 pairs. The pages are rendered from data the running example service answered (clients, requests, status, health); rows it did not have are more rows of the same shape and say so on the page.

HTTPSwitchboard accepts a message in one shape and delivers it in another. Each profile says where a message comes from and where it goes. This page shows how one profile’s settings are read, whether its retries fit inside its lease, and how a profile is put back to “starting” to be checked again. Judge it in the review dialog; formal only. The profile alertmanager is real (it carries Alertmanager alerts from the kyu topic alerts.raw to Home Assistant). uptime-kuma is a mock second profile. The destination’s webhook path is a credential and is never shown. Every request here is faked on the page; nothing is sent.

HTTPSwitchboard takes a message in one shape and delivers it in another. Each profile is one such route: where the message comes from, how it is rewritten, where it goes. This page shows how the profiles part of its status page would look with kp-themes 11.0.0: the main view (a map or cards, you set the default), the path of one profile, and the card that opens on a profile name.

HTTPSwitchboard accepts a message in one shape and delivers it in another. This page shows how its status page could show what happened over the last 24 hours: four key figures with their trend, one strip of hour cells per profile, and the ways the page can stay current.

HTTPSwitchboard accepts a message in one shape and delivers it in another. Its status page shows one row per profile. The real profile is alertmanager: it reads the topic alerts.raw from the kyu hub (subscription switchboard) and delivers to a Home Assistant webhook on homeassistant.lan:8123 (the webhook’s path is a credential and is never shown). The second profile, uptime-kuma, is a mock: it takes POST /uptime-kuma and exists only to show two profiles side by side.
